summary.text: The Atlantic slave trade was the transportation of enslaved African people to the Americas by slave traders.
Europeans set up a coastal slave trade in the 15th century, and trade to the Americas began in the 16th century and lasted well into the 19th.
About 12.75 million Africans were loaded onto slave ships, and up to 2 million of them died during the voyage.

facts.label: Where people came from
facts.value: Most were from Central and West Africa

facts.label: Number loaded
facts.value: About 12.75 million Africans onto slave ships

facts.label: Deaths at sea
facts.value: Up to 2 million died during the voyage

facts.label: Top trading nations
facts.value: Portugal first, then Britain, Spain and France by volume

facts.label: How cargoes were bought
facts.value: Usually purchased from West and Central African merchants

items.prompt: A landowner in the early Americas needs many workers. Why could he not fill the jobs with nearby people or newcomers from home?

options.label: Local people refused paid work, and settlers were barred from landing
Local people were moved away by law, and settlers could not afford the trip
Local people were dying from imported diseases, and few settlers wanted to move yet
Local people were too numerous to hire, and settlers were not needed

items.explain: The sparse indigenous population was shrinking due to European diseases, and Europeans were reluctant to emigrate at this early stage, so slaves were brought from Africa.

items.prompt: A 17th-century ship captain wants a cargo of captives on the African coast. How does he usually obtain them?

options.label: He buys them from West and Central African slave merchants
He sends armed parties inland to seize people himself
He trades with villages that hand over people as tribute
He hires African soldiers to capture them for his ship

items.explain: Slave traders from Europe generally purchased their cargoes from African merchants; European raiding was uncommon and discouraged.

items.prompt: Why did the first people bought by a North European slaver sit confined on board longer than on a Portuguese ship?

options.label: North European ships were slower and took a longer route home
Portuguese ships held fewer people and so left sooner
Authorities in Europe required a waiting period before sailing
The ship itself served as the base for gathering cargo, so it stayed longer on the coast

items.explain: The Portuguese held captives in barracoons ashore, but North European traders used their ship as the base, so ships spent much longer on the African coast.

items.prompt: At a market in the Americas, what determined the price of an enslaved person?

options.label: Their age alone, set by a fixed price list
Their health and how much work they were expected to do
Which African port they had been shipped from
What the buyer's neighbours had paid the year before

items.explain: People were treated as property and sold like merchandise, with prices set by their health and expected productivity.

items.prompt: Someone claims slave trading in Africa began only when Europeans arrived. What does the evidence say?

options.label: The claim is right, since no slavery existed in Africa earlier
Slavery existed but was banned until the Europeans legalized it
Slave trading existed only on the east coast before Europeans came
Slavery was prevalent long before, and European demand gave an existing trade a larger market

items.explain: Slavery was prevalent in many parts of Africa for centuries, and the European demand provided a new and larger market for the already existing trade.

items.prompt: In an English colony in the late 1600s, a baby is born to an enslaved mother. What is the child's legal status?

options.label: The child is also deemed a slave and the property of the mother's owner
The child is free if the father is a free colonist
The child is free but bound to a master for a term of years
The child is free and has legal standing like a contract worker

items.explain: By the middle of the 17th century children born to slave mothers were deemed slaves under the doctrine partus sequitur ventrem, and were legally property.
